==Problem 13==
If <math>n</math> and <math>m</math> are integers and <math>n^2+m^2</math> is even, which of the following is impossible?

<math>\textbf{(A) }</math> <math>n</math> and <math>m</math> are even <math>\qquad\textbf{(B) }</math> <math>n</math> and <math>m</math> are odd <math>\qquad\textbf{(C) }</math> <math>n+m</math> is even <math>\qquad\textbf{(D) }</math> <math>n+m</math> is odd <math>\qquad \textbf{(E) }</math> none of these are impossible

==Solution==
Since <imath>n^2+m^2</imath> is even, either both <imath>n^2</imath> and <imath>m^2</imath> are even, or they are both odd. Therefore, <imath>n</imath> and <imath>m</imath> are either both even or both odd, since the square of an even number is even and the square of an odd number is odd. As a result, <imath>n+m</imath> must be even. The answer, then, is  <imath>n+m</imath>, <imath>\boxed{(\text{D})}</imath>, is odd.

==Solution 2==


We can assign values of n and m as 1,3. Then <imath>1^2 + 3^2</imath> is 10. We can also assign values of n and m to be even, like 2 and 4. After calculating, we can determine that <imath>n^2</imath> + <imath>m^2</imath> could be odd or even. Then, we can conclude that n+m is not odd. Hence our answer choice is <imath>\boxed{(\text{D})}</imath>
- TheNerdWhoIsNerdy.
